author: Augustine
text: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
work: Confessions, Book 1 (Pusey translation)

author: Augustine
text: Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new!
work: Confessions, Book 10 (Pusey translation)

author: Augustine
text: Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt.
work: Confessions, Book 10 (Pusey translation)

author: Augustine
text: Blessed whoso loveth Thee, and his friend in Thee, and his enemy for Thee.
work: Confessions, Book 4 (Pusey translation)

author: Augustine
text: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
work: The City of God, Book 14, Chapter 28 (Dods translation)

author: John Calvin
text: Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid Wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves.
work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 1, Section 1 (Beveridge translation)

author: John Calvin
text: We are not our own; therefore, as far as possible, let us forget ourselves and the things that are ours. On the other hand, we are God's; let us, therefore, live and die to him.
work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, Chapter 7, Section 1 (Beveridge translation)

author: John Calvin
text: Hence we may infer, that the human mind is, so to speak, a perpetual forge of idols.
work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 11, Section 8 (Beveridge translation)

author: John Calvin
text: There is no work so mean and so sordid that does not look truly respectable and highly important in the sight of God.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 94

author: John Calvin
text: Being humbled, we learn to call upon his strength which alone makes us stand up under such a load of afflictions.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 50

author: Martin Luther
text: Faith is a living, daring confidence in God's grace, so sure and certain that a man would stake his life on it a thousand times.
work: Preface to the Epistle to the Romans (1522; Luther's Works vol. 35)

author: Martin Luther
text: That now, I say, upon which you set your heart and put your trust is properly your god.
work: Large Catechism, The First Commandment

author: Martin Luther
text: The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and the grace of God.
work: Ninety-Five Theses (1517), Thesis 62 (Works of Martin Luther, 1915)

author: Martin Luther
text: Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, when He said Poenitentiam agite, willed that the whole life of believers should be repentance.
work: Ninety-Five Theses (1517), Thesis 1 (Works of Martin Luther, 1915)

author: Martin Luther
text: There is no more lovely, friendly and charming relationship, communion or company than a good marriage.
work: Table Talk, no. 292

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, to live with all my might, while I do live.
work: Resolutions, No. 6

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, never to lose one moment of time, but to improve it in the most profitable way I possibly can.
work: Resolutions, No. 5

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, never to do any thing, which I should be afraid to do if it were the last hour of my life.
work: Resolutions, No. 7

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, never to give over, nor in the least to slacken, my fight with my corruptions, however unsuccessful I may be.
work: Resolutions, No. 56

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections.
work: Religious Affections, Part 1

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: Care more for a grain of faith than a ton of excitement.
work: Lectures to My Students, First Series, Lecture 11

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: My trust is not that I am holy, but that, being unholy, Christ died for me.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 592

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: I would rather go to Heaven doubting all the way than be lost through self-confidence.
work: Sermon 2490, "The Danger of Carnal Security"

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: Losses and crosses are heavy to bear; but when our hearts are right with God, it is wonderful how easy the yoke becomes.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 169

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: Jesus was a great worker, and His disciples must not be afraid of hard work.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 128

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult; and left untried.
work: What's Wrong with the World, Part 1, Chapter 5, "The Unfinished Temple"

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: Joy, which was the small publicity of the pagan, is the gigantic secret of the Christian.
work: Orthodoxy, Chapter 9, "Authority and the Adventurer"

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly.
work: Orthodoxy, Chapter 7, "The Eternal Revolution"

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: I would maintain that thanks are the highest form of thought; and that gratitude is happiness doubled by wonder.
work: A Short History of England (1917), p. 59

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: The world will never starve for want of wonders; but only for want of wonder.
work: Tremendous Trifles (1909), Chapter 1

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Aim at Heaven and you will get earth 'thrown in': aim at earth and you will get neither.
work: Mere Christianity, Book 3, Chapter 10, "Hope"

author: C. S. Lewis
text: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world.
work: The Problem of Pain, Chapter 6, "Human Pain"

author: C. S. Lewis
text: There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal.
work: "The Weight of Glory" (1941 sermon), in The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses

author: C. S. Lewis
text: To love at all is to be vulnerable. Love anything, and your heart will certainly be wrung and possibly be broken.
work: The Four Loves, Chapter 6, "Charity"

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Every Christian is to become a little Christ.
work: Mere Christianity, Book 4, Chapter 4, "Good Infection"

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Gratitude looks to the past and love to the present; fear, avarice, lust, and ambition look ahead.
work: The Screwtape Letters (Screwtape speaking)

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of our Church. We are fighting to-day for costly grace.
work: The Cost of Discipleship (1937; English tr. 1959), p. 43

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: Suffering willingly endured is stronger than evil, it spells death to evil.
work: The Cost of Discipleship, p. 142

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: Time is the most precious gift in our possession, for it is the most irrevocable.
work: Letters and Papers from Prison, p. 47

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: We are to find God in what we know, not in what we don't know.
work: Letters and Papers from Prison, letter to Eberhard Bethge, 25 May 1944

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Prayer will consume sin, or sin will choke prayer.
work: A Call to Prayer (1867), p. 16

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Knowledge of the Bible never comes by intuition. It can only be got by hard, regular, daily, attentive, wakeful reading.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Matthew, on Matthew 4:1-11

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Ignorance of Scripture is the root of every error in religion, and the source of every heresy.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. John, Vol. 1, Preface

author: J. C. Ryle
text: The heart is the part of man which God chiefly notices in religion.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Mark, on Mark 7:1-13

author: J. C. Ryle
text: The parent who tries to train without setting a good example is building with one hand and pulling down with the other.
work: The Upper Room, Chapter 16, "The Duties of Parents"

author: John Owen
text: Do you mortify; do you make it your daily work; be always at it whilst you live; cease not a day from this work; be killing sin or it will be killing you.
work: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2

author: John Owen
text: Let not that man think he makes any progress in holiness who walks not over the bellies of his lusts.
work: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2

author: Richard Baxter
text: Take heed to yourselves, lest your example contradict your doctrine ... lest you unsay with your lives, what you say with your tongues.
work: The Reformed Pastor, Chapter 1, Section 1

author: Richard Baxter
text: He that means as he speaks, will surely do as he speaks.
work: The Reformed Pastor, Chapter 1, Section 1

author: Herman Bavinck
text: The essence of the Christian religion consists in the reality that the creation of the Father, ruined by sin, is restored in the death of the Son of God and re-created by the grace of the Holy Spirit into a kingdom of God.
work: Reformed Dogmatics, Vol. 1: Prolegomena, p. 112
